standard.title: Propose actions or responses
standard.description: propose actions or responses to an issue or challenge that consider possible effects of actions
standard.prior_knowledge: From Y2 (AC9HS2S05): Students proposed positive futures for familiar places. From Y1 (AC9HS1S05): Students made proposals for caring for places.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students propose actions or responses to an issue or challenge, considering possible effects of those actions.

nodes.label: Considering effects of actions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can anticipate the effects of proposed actions before committing to them, distinguishing between positive and negative effects.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one positive and one negative effect of a proposed action for a community challenge.
nodes.typical_width: Consider anticipated effects of actions designed to protect or improve places; identify who would be affected by proposed actions and how; distinguish between intended and unintended effects.
wider: Use a consequence wheel to map first- and second-order effects of a proposed action
Compare the effects of two different responses to the same challenge and argue which is better
nodes.hinge_reason: Considering effects before proposing action is the new Year 3 cognitive demand — without this, proposals are wishes rather than considered responses.

response_modes.reason: Effect-consideration requires students to think beyond their preferred outcome — use 'What would happen if...?' scaffolding and consequence wheels.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one positive effect of a proposed action
Identifies at least one negative or unintended effect

nodes.label: Proposing and justifying responses
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a plan of action for a community challenge and argue for their proposal using persuasive reasoning.
nodes.minimum_width: Propose at least one action for a community challenge and give at least one reason why it would help.
nodes.typical_width: Develop plans of action for community challenges (recycling, protecting endangered species, preserving a heritage place, community festival participation); argue a point of view using persuasive language ('I think', 'I dis/agree that').
wider: Develop a group response to a community challenge that considers the perspectives of at least two different community groups
Present a proposal to a real audience (school council, local community member) and respond to questions

response_modes.reason: Action proposals integrate issue analysis, effect consideration, perspective awareness and persuasive communication — the full civic and evaluating demand.

success_criteria: Proposes at least one action for a community challenge
Supports the proposal with at least one persuasive reason
